idiom_name: require / check / assert from the Kotlin standard library
implementation_notes: Kotlin replaces the classic contract scaffold with three stdlib functions whose names state the role: require() for argument and entry conditions (throws IllegalArgumentException), check() for object-state validity (IllegalStateException) and assert() for internal sanity checks that fire only when JVM assertions are enabled with -ea. require and check are inline functions with contracts, so the compiler knows that control flow past the call implies the condition - that smart-cast effect is what makes them the idiomatic invariant carrier. Reach for assert() only for checks you are content to drop from production builds.
pitfalls: require and check throw IllegalArgumentException and IllegalStateException, not AssertionError: catching the wrong type will not catch a violated invariant.
assert() runs only with -ea on the JVM (and is a compile-time flag on Kotlin/Native), so production builds silently skip it.
require/check are inline, so their lambdas are inlined at every call site: heavy predicates inflate bytecode and always run, unlike assert.
Because require/check participate in smart casts, replacing them with manual throw statements can silently break nullability reasoning elsewhere.
